source.title_on_document: InkIdeator: Supporting Chinese-Style Visual Design Ideation via AI-Infused Exploration of Chinese Paintings

paper_design_summary: System paper. Twelve university design and art students each did a Chinese-style book-cover ideation task twice in a remote session, once with InkIdeator (GPT-4o and MidJourney plus AI-annotated keywords on a dataset of Chinese paintings) and once with a baseline (the same painting dataset without the keywords, plus ChatGPT and MidJourney on their own platforms); interfaces and tasks were counterbalanced with a Latin square. Two expert raters scored the clarity and appeal of each verbally presented idea, and participants answered Creativity Support Index and design-goal questionnaire items.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two interfaces (InkIdeator, baseline) and of the two task themes, counterbalanced with a Latin square; every participant used both interfaces
assignment.quote: Participants were asked to complete design ideation tasks twice in two settings, i.e., InkIdeator and baseline. We counterbalanced the tasks and interfaces using Latin Square.

arms.name: InkIdeator
arms.description: Symbol Association Panel, Image Library with AI-annotated keywords, Moodboard, and Image Generation Panel (GPT-4o prompts to MidJourney)

arms.name: Baseline
arms.description: Image search on the same annotated Chinese-painting dataset and a moodboard, with the annotated keywords not displayed; ChatGPT and Midjourney used on their original platforms

participants.who: 12 university students with a design or art background and prior Chinese-style visual design experience (10 design majors, 2 art majors; 11 female, 1 male; mean age 21.83); each served in both conditions
participants.quote: We recruited 12 participants (denoted as P01-P12, 11 females, 1 male; age M = 21.83 and SD = 2.03) through an online recruitment posting in a university
participants.locator: p. 11, Section 6.2; p. 12, Table 4; N = 12 also in Figure 10 caption, p. 14

ai_tool.name_model: InkIdeator (GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, MidJourney API) vs baseline with ChatGPT and Midjourney
ai_tool.how_used: InkIdeator suggests cultural symbols for the theme, shows AI-annotated keywords on example paintings, and generates sketches from selected keywords; the baseline offers the same painting search without keywords and the general tools on their own platforms

task.description: Ideate a Chinese-style illustration for a book cover on the theme "Environmental Protection" or "Aerospace"; the outcome is an idea presented verbally with references (paintings, generated images)
task.duration: Approximately 35 minutes, no more than 40 minutes, per ideation task (p. 11, Section 6.3).

outcomes.name: Clarity and appeal of the idea description (Q1)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two external raters with graduate degrees in design and Chinese-style design experience rated each verbally described idea with its visual references on a 7-point clarity-and-appeal scale. If their scores differed by more than two points, they discussed whether to adjust them; the final output score averaged their post-discussion scores. The 24 outputs came from the same 12 people completing both conditions (p. 12, Section 6.4).

contrasts.reported: InkIdeator 5.83 (SD 1.09) vs Baseline 5.50 (SD 1.46) on a 7-point scale; paired-sample t-test, p = 0.254; within-subjects, N = 12

InkIdeator 4.92 (1.24) vs Baseline 3.92 (1.08); Wilcoxon signed-rank Z = -2.360, p = 0.018

studies.label: Formative interviews on Chinese-style visual design ideation

assignment.what_was_assigned: No experimental AI allocation or condition comparison; participants were recruited by snowballing for qualitative interviews. Experimental assignment structure is not applicable.
assignment.quote: We conducted one-hour semi-structured interviews with each participant via a video-conferencing app.

arms.name: Interview cohort
arms.description: Remote interviews about ideation practices, challenges and attitudes toward GenAI; no study-administered AI assistance condition.

participants.who: Ten interviewees (S01-S10), including a Chinese painter, college Chinese-painting teachers, art and design students and a painting apprentice. Some subsequently helped with system validation; S02 and S03 also took part in the extended use cases. These are not additional participants in S1.
participants.quote: In total, we recruited ten participants via snowballing starting from S01 and S08 (Table 1).
participants.locator: p. 4, Sections 3-3.1 and Table 1; pp. 7-8, Section 4.2; p. 10, Section 5.2; p. 15, Section 8

ai_tool.name_model: GenAI tools such as Midjourney discussed in interviews; no assigned intervention
ai_tool.how_used: Participants described prior practices and attitudes toward GenAI; the formative study did not compare AI-assisted creative outputs.

task.description: Semi-structured interviews on learning from Chinese paintings for visual design, ideation challenges and perceptions of GenAI. No creativity or diversity outcome was scored on participant output (pp. 4-6, Sections 3.1-3.4).

studies.label: Painting-corpus mining and qualitative validation of AI annotations

assignment.what_was_assigned: No people were assigned to AI assistance. An existing painting corpus was classified and annotated; evaluators examined different paintings and annotation dimensions. Experimental assignment structure is not applicable.
assignment.quote: each annotator was assigned different paintings with different focuses.

arms.name: AI-annotated painting corpus
arms.description: Existing Chinese paintings classified with MambaVision features and annotated with GPT-4o mini; no human creative-task arm.

participants.who: No analyzed sample of people creating outputs under an AI condition is reported. The qualitative annotation evaluators were S05 and two additional Chinese-painting students, S11 and S12; these three people were raters, not creative-task participants. S05 also participated in the formative study.
participants.quote: We invited S05 and another two Chinese painting students (a fourth-year student and a PhD student, denoted as S11 and S12) to evaluate the MLLM-annotated performance.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o mini; MambaVision for painting classification; bert-base-chinese for concept clustering
ai_tool.how_used: Models classified existing paintings, generated labels for their cultural and visual dimensions, and supported clustering of annotated concepts (pp. 6-8, Sections 4.2-4.3).

task.description: Mining a corpus of 16,315 Chinese paintings (p. 6, Section 4.1), followed by qualitative validation of annotations on 44 paintings by S05, S11 and S12 (p. 8, Section 4.2.3). These are painting counts, not people counts. Annotation accuracy and corpus-description results do not measure human creative performance or changes in diversity across people; no outcome addresses the three atlas questions.

studies.label: Evaluation of AI-generated cultural symbols, design intentions, images and poems

assignment.what_was_assigned: The same tag sets were used for InkIdeator and a direct-Midjourney image-generation baseline. Tags and some image-prompt sets were randomly sampled; this was model-input sampling, not random assignment of people to AI assistance.
assignment.quote: we directly prompt Midjourney with the selected tags and additionally include the tag “Chinese painting” to generate images as a baseline condition.
assignment.locator: p. 10, Section 5.2 and Table 3; p. 20, Appendix B

arms.name: InkIdeator model pipeline
arms.description: GPT-4o generates cultural symbols and design intentions; MidJourney generates images from the design intentions; GPT-4o mini supplies poems for images.

arms.name: Direct Midjourney baseline
arms.description: Midjourney is prompted directly with the selected tags plus the keyword Chinese painting; used for the generated-image comparison.

participants.who: Three Chinese-painting-trained raters (S04, S06 and S11) evaluated model-generated content. They were not participants producing AI-assisted creative work; creator sample counts are therefore left null. S04 and S06 were formative interviewees, and S11 also evaluated annotations in S3.
participants.quote: We invited three raters with training in Chinese paintings (i.e., S04, S06 in Table 1 and S11 in section 4) to evaluate the quality of the AI generated content
participants.locator: p. 10, Section 5.2 and Table 3; p. 4, Table 1; p. 8, Section 4.2.3

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini and MidJourney API
ai_tool.how_used: The authors generated evaluation stimuli from design themes and randomly sampled tags. Raters judged the resulting model content (p. 10, Section 5.2; p. 20, Appendix B).

task.description: Evaluate 20 cultural-symbol sets and 20 image-generation tag sets, with three generated images per tag set and image prompts for five sets (p. 10, Section 5.2; p. 20, Appendix B). Table 3 reports 5-point ratings of symbol relevance and variety, design-intention relevance, image relevance, preference, aesthetics and within-set variety, and poem relevance. These model-output ratings address none of the three human-creativity questions; variety among symbols or generated images is not diversity across different people.

studies.label: Extended use cases with experienced Chinese painters

assignment.what_was_assigned: Two painters used InkIdeator on self-chosen ink-wash painting ideas and thought aloud; no comparison condition or randomized allocation. Experimental assignment structure is not applicable.
assignment.quote: we invited two experienced Chinese painters (S02, S03 in Table 1, noted as E1 and E2 in this section) to use InkIdeator for 40 minutes

arms.name: InkIdeator
arms.description: Qualitative use of InkIdeator to develop ideas for ink-wash Chinese paintings.

participants.who: Two experienced Chinese painters, E1 and E2, who are S02 and S03 from the formative interviews (S2); Table 1 identifies both as college Chinese-painting teachers. These are reused formative participants, not additional participants in S1.
participants.quote: we invited two experienced Chinese painters (S02, S03 in Table 1, noted as E1 and E2 in this section) to use InkIdeator for 40 minutes
participants.locator: p. 15, Section 8; p. 4, Table 1; p. 16, Figures 12-13

ai_tool.how_used: Painters explored examples and annotated tags, associated cultural symbols, and generated visual references while developing their own painting ideas (pp. 15-16, Section 8).

task.description: Think aloud while developing self-selected ink-wash painting ideas. The paper presents process observations, perceptions and illustrative outputs, without a scored creativity or across-person diversity outcome (pp. 15-16, Section 8 and Figures 12-13).

eligibility.reason: The main comparison analyzed 12 unique people, each in both AI conditions (p. 11, Sections 6.1-6.2; p. 14, Figure 10), below the codebook threshold of 50. The 24 scored ideation outputs are not 24 independent people (p. 12, Section 6.4). Tasks and interfaces were counterbalanced with a Latin square, but randomized condition order is not stated (p. 11, Section 6.3; p. 12, Figure 7), so criterion 1 remains unclear and the design is other. Expert-rated clarity and appeal satisfies the output-scored criterion; the CSI items are self-reports (p. 12, Section 6.4). The formative interviews and extended use cases provide no qualifying scored-outcome comparison (p. 4, Section 3; pp. 15-16, Section 8). Corpus annotation and model-output evaluations are model_only; their raters, painting counts and generated-image variety do not add randomized creators or an across-person diversity outcome (pp. 6-10, Sections 4-5.2; p. 20, Appendix B). No study qualifies for the core dataset or an AI-versus-human, observational or synthesis context class; retain the paper in the screening report as a small experiment with randomization unstated.
